# High Idle on Fuel Injected Motorcycle

A Honda Grom MSX125 surging up to 6,000 RPM with no air leaks, free throttle cables, and a clean fuel system is a classic symptom of an Electronic Control Unit (ECU) that has lost synchronization with the actual engine position. When you reset the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) and the idle returns to normal for a week before drifting back, the issue isn't mechanical binding; it's data drift or a specific calibration sequence that hasn't been permanently addressed.

The core problem lies in how modern fuel-injected engines manage idle speed. The ECU relies on input from the TPS to determine when you are not accelerating and should cut fuel to maintain base idle. If the ECU thinks the throttle is slightly open when it's actually closed, or if the "closed" position has drifted away from the learned baseline, the engine will rev higher than intended. On many Honda engines of this generation, a simple reset often relearns the current state but fails to clear the long-term fuel trim or idle learn values stored in non-volatile memory, causing the value to revert over time.

To resolve this permanently, you need to force the ECU into a full initialization mode that clears learned values and recalibrates the TPS zero point against the mechanical stop. This process differs from a standard diagnostic reset. The procedure typically involves cutting power to the ignition completely while holding the starter button for a specific duration (often 10 seconds) or utilizing the specific "idle learn" sequence found in the service manual for your model year. Some units require you to disconnect the battery for at least 15 minutes to ensure all capacitors discharge and volatile memory clears before reconnecting.

While performing this reset, verify the electrical resistance of the TPS potentiometer. Even if the cable moves freely, the internal track on the potentiometer can develop a dead zone or inconsistent resistance curve. If the ECU reads a voltage that corresponds to 50% throttle even when the lever is fully closed, the high idle will return immediately after the reset because the ECU has no choice but to compensate for that perceived acceleration. Use a multimeter to measure the voltage at the TPS connector with the ignition on and the throttle closed; it should read near 0V or the specific baseline defined in the service data for your ECU version.

Another common pitfall is ignoring the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve, which is physically integrated into the intake manifold on these bikes. Unlike older carbureted systems that used a separate valve, the Grom uses an electronic stepper motor to control airflow at idle. If this motor is clogged with carbon buildup or the gears are stripped, the ECU cannot maintain the target RPM. Even if you have added Redex to your fuel and cleaned the injectors, the air path remains the critical variable here. A sticky IAC valve will cause the engine to hunt for a stable idle, often settling at a much higher speed before finally dropping or stalling.

When addressing the TPS reset issue, remember that this is an electronic calibration, not a mechanical adjustment. Do not try to force the throttle body closed tightly against the stop bolt; this can damage the internal spline of the stepper motor or warp the plastic throttle plates. The goal is to let the ECU learn the exact physical position of the "closed" state relative to the electrical signal it receives. If the high idle returns within a week, re-check your wiring harness for chafed wires near the clutch lever pivot point, where vibration often breaks insulation and creates intermittent short circuits that fool the ECU into thinking the throttle is open.
